+*Feedback from wider Privacy team:*+

Usually, we send a message to the driver to confirm that we can disclose the information to the driver. In this case, it could have been reasonable to refer the FO to the driver or driver’s relatives, not Bolt. This is not the information that is stored only at Bolt and no one knows it.

*Steps:*

# Agree that we can ask for the PoA or a signed agreement to act on behalf of the driver
# If no, I suppose it’s 90% chance, let’s state that we cannot disclose driver’s personal data without authority or driver’s consent and refer them to the driver’s relatives
# Of course, we can potentially rely on the legal basis - in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person - but it’s doable whether the driver is really in a hospital + what his condition is, eg he cannot give consent to this request

----

Good day,

Thank you for the data subject request that you submitted on behalf of Costin Popescu, which was received by us on 9 August 2024.

To help us ensure the security of the personal data we hold, we need to verify your legal authority to submit this request on behalf of Costin Popescu. We accept any of the following as proof of your legal authority: a written consent signed by the data subject; or a certified copy of a power of attorney; or other proof of authorization. Your request did not include proof of legal authority.

Please be aware that we are unable to respond to your request until we receive the additional information specified above. The deadline of one month to respond to your request will be paused until we have received the additional information. Please can you provide the additional information requested by replying to this email. We appreciate your cooperation in this matter and look forward to receiving the requested information from you.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

The way we were using MqDbSimplePublisher for status updates caused user impacting issues on daily basis, and it was show-stopper for migration to TiDB:

* the publishing table is almost empty most of the time time, with high number of inserts/deletes
* the publishing table is being polled in short cycles all the time
* TiDB uses soft-deletes & data garbage collection, i.e. before the garbage collection kicks-in the table contain large amounts of data, most of the records soft deleted
* TiDB is fully distributed - indices maintenance is expensive and it’s going on all the time

As result:

* MqDbSimplePublisher running in short cycles (to achieve “low” latency required by the involved UI flow) was getting stuck, causing busy neighborhood issues (garbage data collection, constant index rebuilding) to other DBs on the cluster, and pushing event loop lag up causing secondary issues to other flows (typically timeouts)

TL;DR:  MqDbSimplePublisher doesn’t scale up well, and to use DB involving polling in a flow where we are trying to achieve “low” latency is a broken idea.

Just as reminder why we decided to decomm MqDbSimplePublisher from this (and other) flow.

*Update for the Business on the Dutch AP Decision against Uber*  
{panel}

*Privacy Team Update: Uber's GDPR Case in the Netherlands*You may know that Uber was recently fined by the Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) for not complying with GDPR rules when transferring personal data from the EU to the U.S. But what actually happened, and what does it mean for Bolt?*Origin of the case*

* The investigation began after complaints from French Uber drivers who were concerned that their personal data was being transferred to the U.S. without proper protection.
* The complaints were initially submitted to the French data protection authority (CNIL), and later forwarded them to the Dutch AP as Uber B.V., the entity responsible for the processing activities in the EU, is based in the Netherlands.

*What Happened?*

* Uber was found to have violated GDPR by transferring data to the U.S. without appropriate safeguards. Uber’s data flows involved sending personal data from the EU to its U.S. headquarters, where it was processed centrally. Initially, Uber relied on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) to legally justify these transfers, but the pivotal moment came when Uber decided to remove these SCCs in August 2021, believing they were no longer necessary. As a result, Uber unlawfully transferred personal data from the EEA to the USA between August 2021 to November 2023.
* The AP fined Uber €290,000,000 for this violation. This amount was justified by the AP based on the seriousness of the violation, its prolonged duration, the sensitive nature of the data involved, and the need for the fine to be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive.

*Uber’s Argument:*

* *No "Transfer":* Uber claimed that since UTI in the U.S. was directly subject to GDPR and French drivers submitted their data directly to UTI, it didn’t constitute an international transfer.
* *Removal of SCCs:* Believing additional safeguards like SCCs were unnecessary, Uber removed them in August 2021.

*The views of the Dutch Data Protection Authority*:

* *There was a "Transfer":* The AP argued that this data movement did qualify as an international transfer under GDPR, requiring compliance with Chapter V.
* *Need for SCCs:* The AP insisted that SCCs were essential to ensure French drivers could enforce GDPR obligations against UTI in the U.S.

*Appeal of the Decision:*

* Uber will likely appeal the decision.
* The key disagreements would likely be about whether Chapter V of the GDPR applies, how "transfer" is defined, and whether removing the safeguards (SCCs) was lawful.

*What does it mean for Bolt?*:

* *Centralised Data Storage in the EEA*: Since Bolt stores its data centrally in the EEA, it avoids many of the challenges Uber faced with U.S. data transfers.
* *SCCs between Bolt entities*: Bolt currently enters into SCCs between Bolt entities/local Partners when launching in new markets. Since the _Schrems II_ decision, Bolt has never removed SCCs from these types of agreements.
* *Local entities and 3rd parties*: It is important to remember that when Bolt sends data to a local Bolt entity or shares data with a third-party service provider, Bolt is required to comply with GDPR rules! Bolt has template Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) and Data Sharing Agreements (DSAs) in place which include SCCs.

*Recommendation*

* Our preference should always be to store personal data within the EEA, especially where Bolt uses cloud services from third-parties (e.g. Box, Microsoft 365, etc). Most SaaS/cloud service providers offer 'regions' that can be selected to store data and we must always ensure that we leverage these options.
* It is vital that Privacy is looped into any agreement or partnership that involves the transfer of personal data so that a DPA/DSA and SCCs can be incorporated. Never assume that the contract provided by a third party includes all the necessary provisions, including SCCs!
* {{The Privacy Team will be doing a reconciliation to determine whether there are any historical inter-company agreements that don't have the required SCCs in place.}}

_If you have any questions on this case, feel free to reach out to a Privacy badger._

As for how to avoid those rare occasions where AWS client-lib built-in fail-and-retry mechanism fails.

It is briefly mentioned in  [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/94623|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/94623|smart-link]  description, for more details see:

* [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaScriptSDK/v3/latest/Package/-smithy-util-retry/Variable/DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS/|https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaScriptSDK/v3/latest/Package/-smithy-util-retry/Variable/DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS/] 
* [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html|https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html|smart-link] 

By default retries 3 times with exponential back-off before it gives up. That can be configured.

So to make the publishing more robust (my order of preference):

* tune the AWS client-lib params so it retries more than 3 times => if it is in some way exposed/possible in the Bolt framework; that might require PINT discussion
* fail the after-commit hook in case the publishing fails, pushing the responsibility to retry to the caller - problem there is that the publishing happens after commit, i.e. retrying will re-execute the DB part and hence it must be idempotent
* implement some custom re-try mechanism without storing - if we for whatever reason can’t tune the AWS client-lib build-in mechanism for the same
* implement some custom retry mechanism with storing - that could be either SQS DLQ or DB (store on failure and have a separate mechanism to re-publish from the storage)

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Detailed summary of the Decision (for internal purposes - not to be shared with the Business)*
{panel}

*Chapter 1: Introduction to the Investigation*The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) initiated an investigation into Uber's compliance with GDPR, focusing on data transfers from the EU to the U.S. The investigation was triggered by complaints from French Uber drivers following the SCHREMS II ruling, which invalidated the Privacy Shield._Key Points_:

* *SCHREMS II Impact*: Raised concerns over Uber's compliance with GDPR in data transfers.
* *Chapter V GDPR*: Central issue was compliance with data transfer regulations.
* *Alleged Violation*: Uber was found to have violated Article 44 of the GDPR.
* *Investigation Process*: Involved notifications, an investigation report, and Uber's responses.

*Chapter 2: Facts and Circumstance*This chapter details Uber's data processing activities, focusing on the joint responsibility of Uber B.V. and Uber Technologies Inc. for handling personal data within the EEA and the transfer of this data to the U.S. Uber's decision to remove Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and subsequent certification under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework are also discussed._Key Points_:

* *Joint Controllers*: Uber B.V. and UTI are jointly responsible for data processing within the EEA.
* *Centralized IT*: Data is processed on UTI's servers in the U.S., raising GDPR concerns.
* *SCC Removal*: Uber removed SCCs, arguing that the data was not technically "transferred" under GDPR and that UTI in the USA was in any event subject directly to the GDPR by virtue of Art 3(2).
* *EU-US Privacy Framework*: Uber later certified under this framework to ensure compliance.

*Chapter 3: Uber's Perspective*Uber defended its actions, arguing that Chapter V of the GDPR does not apply since Article 3 already covers the data processing. Uber also challenged the interpretation of 'transfer' and asserted that its actions were lawful under Article 49 exceptions._Key Points_:

* *Non-Applicability of Chapter V*: Uber claims Chapter V doesn't apply due to Article 3 coverage.
* *Transfer Definition*: Uber contests the definition and applicability of 'transfer' under GDPR.
* *Legal Compliance*: Uber argues that even if a transfer occurred, it was lawful under GDPR exceptions.

*Chapter 4: Assessment*The AP assessed Uber's activities, determining that both Article 3 and Chapter V of the GDPR apply. The AP rejected Uber's argument about international obligations and concluded that the data transfers required appropriate safeguards under GDPR._Key Points_:

* *Joint Controllers*: Uber B.V. and UTI are jointly responsible under GDPR.
* *Territorial Scope*: Article 3 and Chapter V of the GDPR are complementary and both apply.
* *Legal Framework*: The AP applied GDPR criteria to assess the legality of Uber's data transfers.

*Chapter 5: The Fine*The AP imposed a €290,000,000 fine on Uber for violating GDPR, based on the seriousness and duration of the violation. The fine was calculated to be effective, proportionate, and deterrent._Key Points_:

* *Fine Calculation*: Based on the gravity, duration, and impact of the infringement.
*  *Final Fine*: Set at €290,000,000 after considering mitigating and aggravating factors.
* *Proportionality*: The fine was intended to ensure future compliance and prevent violations.

*Chapter 6: Decision*The AP concluded by imposing the fine on Uber for violating Article 44 of the GDPR. Uber has six weeks to pay the fine or appeal the decision._Key Points_:

* *Imposition of Fine*: €290,000,000 for GDPR violations.
* *Seriousness*: The violation was significant due to its duration and the data involved.
* *Payment and Appeal*: Uber must pay within six weeks or appeal to the District Court of The Hague.

{{Potential Key Areas of Disagreement in an Appeal}}If Uber appeals the decision, the key areas of disagreement that would likely be reviewed by the courts include:

# *Applicability of Chapter V*: Uber's primary argument is that Chapter V of the GDPR should not apply since Article 3 already covers the data processing activities. Uber contends that simultaneous application is redundant and unnecessary. The AP disagrees, viewing Chapter V as complementary to Article 3 and essential to maintaining the high level of data protection required under GDPR.
# *Interpretation of 'Transfer'*: Uber argues that the concept of 'transfer' is not clearly defined within the GDPR and that the European Data Protection Board's (EDPB) interpretation is not binding. Uber maintains that the data was not technically 'transferred' since the data subjects themselves provided their data directly to UTI. The AP, however, considers these activities as data transfers that require compliance with Chapter V.
# *Legality of SCC Removal*: Uber’s decision to remove SCCs based on its interpretation of the GDPR will be scrutinized. Uber believes that the updated SCCs indicated that they should not be used when the importer (UTI) is subject to the GDPR under Article 3. The AP views this removal as non-compliance, leading to the significant fine.
# *Use of Article 49 Exceptions*: Uber's reliance on Article 49 exceptions for data transfers will be a point of contention. The AP might argue that these exceptions are not intended for long-term use or repeated transfers, while Uber contends that their application was lawful and necessary.

Increasing retry count in AWS client-lib goes not solve the problem. No matter how many retries we have there is still a chance that they all will fail.

I think the following algorithm should work:

# Do some logic.
# Store the result into DB with some state like {{exporting}}.
# Send SNS event.
# Update the result state to {{exported}}.

In happy case these 4 steps are executed, and that’s all.

In case if SNS sending fails, error is thrown and step 4 is not executed. And then we need some cron which looks for records with {{exporting}} state with some delay and retries sending SNS event. If sending event was successful, then it updates the state to {{exported}}, if not, then there is an error thrown and the same record will be picked up by the next cron run.

In this case we don’t need to run cron too often, because it is only for not happy cases which happen rarely. We also need to ensure that this cron doesn’t pick up records with {{exporting}} state too early to not interfere with happy flow. For this we can use, e.g. {{last_update}} column and look for records with {{exporting}} state which were updated no later than 10 seconds in the past.

I think this approach is close to the second point from the list in previous comment.

Hey! Sorry for the delay in getting back to you!

This FO doesn't have to pay anything to us :) I see the fleet balance had become negative on 28th of July, when the drivers had a lot of cash rides - so more commission added to the balance than in-app payments. And by the 31st there still had been more cash rides than in-app. But if you look at the fleet weekly balance, you can see that by the end of the same week the balance was already positive and they even had a payout.

 So nothing to worry about for the FO, and in 90% of the cases they can ignore this sum on the invoice. If they also don't get any payouts from us - then the neg balance should be addressed.


_In addition just for general information:
Just from previous experience in mixed payment method markets, although in EU drivers and fleets don't really get into debt, if either the FO or you notice one driver in the fleet doing more cash rides than the others then it needs attention. keep in mind that if one driver in the fleet is in debt at the end of the week, FO will get less money than what they will have to pay to the other drivers - debt for fleet driver is between the FO and the Driver, we cannot help there (only by switching off cash payments). For example
Driver 1 earned 250 PLN
Driver 2 earned 100 PLN
Driver 3 earned -200 PLN (because he was taking mostly cash rides)
FO payout will be 150 PLN but he has to pay to the driver 1 and 2 350, so the 200 from his pocket until the driver 3 pays him back.

Hope it makes sense :) _

* This change will significantly increase the CS cost. Currently, the CS contact reason {{I want to change my banking details}} is the second popular among the payout-related CS tickets tag (up to 50% of the tickets). Thailand is one of the biggest markets with ~400 payout-related CS contacts per week. As a result, the number of contacts may grow 50% to 800 contacts per week/40k additional contacts per year.
* This change will shift the responsibility from the partners to the CS agents who change the bank details. In case of a CS agent mistake, we will have to compensate a missing payout to the driver.
* Instead of disabling the self service, I propose to:
** Investigate the situation and measure the monetary impact of duplicate accounts. 
** Improve the duplicate account detection algorithm and develop a procedure allowing to detect and block duplicated account.

Unfortunately, we do not have the draft of the Country Addendum (only its template) but my understanding is that Hertz France (and not Hertz UK) will be the party in its agreement. Saying that I think that from VAT PoV we need to confirm that

* Hertz signing Country Addendum is Hertz FR and know it legal status in FR (local entity or VAT registration)
* *Nature of the Minimum Revenue Guarantee.* Everything what is not the delivery of the goods falls under the definition of the delivery of the service. Therefore, if we base only on master agreement - my questions from May whether we deal with financial or operational lease remain. Why? Because financial leasing is treated as the delivery of services, while operational - delivery of goods.

If the MRG were limited solely to bringing Hertz's income to the established minimum, it wouldn't pose a significant problem (general rule of taxation → reverse charge in EE). However, this fee also applies to situations where the driver has not paid their leasing instalments. If that's the case, then we are dealing with the assumption of the payment obligation by Bolt, and we're talking about a leasing service. Therefore, it is crucial to know what type of leasing we're referring to. I also suggest clarifying in the contract what is covered under MRG. On the other hand, if we leave the wide definition, it would be easier to defend the service taxed based on the general rule of taxation. But if the invoice is issued by Hertz FR for the revenue limited to the territory of FR only, one may argue that the service is limited to FR thus taxed in FR.

If it is correct from FR tax law then:

# Domestic VAT because seller is established and customer not established in PT. (If Hertz is not established in FR and Bolt Ops has FR VAT ID then we would have domestic reverse charge)
# VAT deductible because it is not related to hiring of vehicles (VAT deduction limited on car-related expenses)

HELENA WDYT?

Another option is to treat the _transaction between Hertz and Bolt as equal to leasing payment._ Then I imagine that the flow would look like:

Hertz invoice to the driver for 30EUR but minimum revenue shall be 40EUR so

Hertz invoice to Bolt for 10EUR



But MRG covers also situations where the driver doesn’t pay his instalments. It is not clear for me if Hertz will include such debt in its invoice cumulatively. Even if yes, we would need to have an annex to see the split and in case of audit tax treatment may be challenged.

Hertz invoice to the driver for 30EUR but driver didn’t pay

Hertz credit note to the driver for 30EUR

Hertz invoice to Bolt for 40EUR (30EUR unpaid instalment + 10EUR to even the minimum revenue)



Alternative option: _Bolt as the guarantor of the leasing._ No service for consideration between Hertz and Bolt. Do you think it would be the option? I doubt but sharing this idea to have your opinion. Especially in the countries, like FR, which include in the VAT code (art.256) that obligations to refrain from an act or to tolerate a situation is a delivery of the service.



Invoicing part, we can touch when we know the final treatment but as a rule of thumb, invoices issued to Bolt shall go via TELEMA.



Additional point: are we going to charge any fee or increase commission invoice because of MSG? Then we could state that we act as a guarantor of the payment on behalf of the driver.



France does not have a legal definition of “effective use and enjoyment” of intangible services. The most “logical” scenario seems to be as follow:

Hertz FR invoice with local standard VAT issued to BOLT OPS FR

Bolt has full VAT recovery rights but above I have shared with you all my thoughts because of the lack of the clear definition of MSG which impacts the place of taxation.

{quote}> What is the main goal for you to use Driver Audit view?

The main goal for us in using the Driver Audit view is to ensure the quality of our registrations. We use it to check for any mistakes made during the registration process, verify that all documents and information are accurate, and correct any errors that may have occurred.

> How many drivers you audit during the day in total for GE market?

The number of drivers we audit daily for the GE market can vary widely depending on the workload for that day. There are times when we conduct bulk audits, and in those cases, we might process 200-300 drivers in a single day. On other days, the number could be considerably lower. For instance, when I use the Audit function, I usually handle 20-30 drivers at a time. However, the total number of drivers audited each day really depends on the specific demands and the volume of registrations we need to review.

As far as I am aware, this process is not enforced by law in Georgia.{quote}

This can also impact customer support, as they may receive more tickets from drivers needing corrections, such as fixing incorrect car registration numbers. # *Implement Appropriate Safeguards:*

* Perform a TIA to evaluate the risks of transferring personal data to Hong Kong or Mainland China.

* Ensure that suppliers in Hong Kong adhere to GDPR standards through robust contractual obligations.

* Develop and implement a strategy to manage data breach notifications in Hong Kong, considering the lack of mandatory requirements.
* Ensure timely responses to data breaches by the supplier to avoid non-compliance with GDPR timelines.

# *Monitor Government Surveillance Risks:*

* Continuously assess and monitor the impact of China's Cybersecurity Law and National Intelligence Law on data privacy and security.
* Evaluate the effects of Hong Kong's 2020 National Security Law on government surveillance and align practices to mitigate risks.

With this information it is possible to create a “Flow” that sends more customizable Whatsapp and SMS messages (and maybe even initiate phone calls).Example:

# Reminder Whatsapp message is sent 1 h before the start date and time of the video call
# If the Whatsapp message is not received within 2 min, an SMS is sent

Hey! Can we please confirm one additional step with the local team to ensure whatever information we have on the company profile matches with the document set tied to the company. Marked this as *“step five”*.

*Step one:* Check if the person who sent the message is indeed a fleet owner ([Fleet Owner verification|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/8671806622098#verifying-fleet-owners]). If the person contacting us a is a private driver, de-escalate to Tier 1.

*Step two:* Ask for -a picture of the fleet owner holding an official document,- a recent “Extrait KBIS” of the fleet, and an IBAN proof manually signed by the fleet owner.

*-Step three:-* -Verify if the person in the selfie is the fleet owner of the fleet that the banking details will be changed.-

*Step three:* Verify the validity of the RIB via [https://www.ibancalculator.com/|https://www.ibancalculator.com/|smart-link].

*Step four:* Update the RIB on the fleet’s profile and run the macro on all drivers’ profiles using [https://ui.vision/|https://ui.vision/|smart-link]

*Step five:* Upload the new IBAN proof document received form the fleet owner as part of the company document set. Document type “fo_rib”.

*Step six*: check a few driver accounts to make sure the change has taken effect. Then reply to the fleet owner with a confirmation that the RIB has been changed.

Thanks [~accountid:5e3d437d9749d00c924cb0f5] - I have reviewed the below and my thoughts are as follows. In short, the majority of the below types of request do not necessarily need to be escalated to Privacy, and can be dealt with by CS. 

{color:#4c9aff}*We can assist with CS Knowledge Management with preparing an article*{color} on how to deal with these, which would include steps and different templates that CS can leverage. In the meantime, I include a high-level overview below.

----

{color:#36b37e}*Issues / Requests / Questions that can be dealt with by CS (and summarised in a KB article)*{color}

* *I want to know more about my Rider Rating (i.e., requests for* +*general info*+ *about rider ratings)* (1627 tickets last year)
** e.g., “_Can you explain to me how rider ratings are calculated?_”
*** +Rationale+: These are not privacy questions, as they are generic questions about how the feature functions. They can be dealt with relatively quickly by referring the rider to relevant informative materials.
*** +CS Response+: Refer the rider to the blog post and include a brief explanation of how the feature works (e.g. “_Please note that your Rider Rating as it appears in your Bolt app is calculated as an average rating based on your ratings from the previous 365 days. Each rating is from 1 to 5, as provided by the driver at the end of each trip. Further information on Rider Ratings can be found here:_ [https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/|https://bolt.eu/en/rider-rating/|smart-link].”)
* *I want to know why my Rider rating dropped* (1574 tickets last year)
** e.g., “_Hello. I was deducted a point from the rating, please tell me why?_” or “_Why did my rating drop? It was always 5_”
*** +Rationale+: Again, this is not necessarily a privacy question. Also, Bolt has no control over how a driver may rate a rider, and so we can (to an extent) standardise our responses here.
*** +CS Response+: Use a similar response to the above, but also refer to the Marketplace Conduct guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link] ) and say that the ratings drop when the drivers rate them (i.e., Bolt cannot control this).
** e.g., “_Rider see her rating differently than we see in admin._”
*** +Rationale+: I am dealing with a similar query from CS ([here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-37847]). The difference is that the app only shows an average rating from the _last 365 days_, which is different to the calculation in Admin. The user would never pick up on this difference, it is just something for CS to be aware of.
*** +CS Response+: There would not be a response to the _user_ in this context. CS should just be made aware in the relevant knowledge article that the rating in Admin (which is not visible to the rider) is different to the rating in the App (which is visible to the rider).
* *I want to increase my Rider rating* (805 tickets last year)
** e.g., “_how can we solve the problem of drivers who underestimate the ratings_” or “_it looks like driver had given me a 1* star rating, so it will affect my rating for the future rides. Is that possible to remove its ? All the evidence will be provided if needed_”
*** +Rationale+: Again, this is not really a privacy question. It is also not up to Bolt to manually change rider ratings, as they are at the driver’s discretion. As such, we can (to an extent) standardise our responses here.
*** +CS Response+: Use a similar response to the above, but also refer to the Marketplace Conduct guidelines ([https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/marketplace-guidelines-terms/|smart-link] ) and make it clear that ratings are at the driver’s discretion and cannot be controlled by Bolt.

----

{color:#ff5630}*Issues / Requests / Questions that should be escalated to Privacy*{color}

To be clear - we would mention  summarise these types of cases in the same KB article, but with explicit instructions that they should be escalated to Privacy.

* *Visibility of the Rider Rating*
** e.g. “_Is the passenger rating visible? In this way, you give the drivers the opportunity to give a bad rating to the passengers who reported the rides_” or “_With Bolt I could always see my ratings from the drivers in the app, but that is no longer possible! ! Why is that?_”
*** +Rationale+: Over the past 12 months, Privacy managed an inquiry with the Estonian data protection regulator that included this issue (i.e., the rating needed to be turned off in certain jurisdictions temporarily, and other permanently). We should therefore carefully control what we say in this regard. This would be the same if the request related to the impact that Rider Ratings have on blocking users / penalising them.
*** +CS Response+: Escalate to Privacy. We will review and prepare the response.
* *Requests pertaining to individual ratings*
** e.g., “_What was my rating for this trip_” or “_I would like all the rider ratings ever given to me_”
*** +Rationale+: This is technically a data subject access request. As such, this is something Privacy should handle.
*** +Privacy Response+: Escalate to Privacy. We will review and prepare the response.
* *Issues / requests / questions that explicitly mention either: (a) data protection law; and/or (b) personal data processing*
** e.g., “_How is my personal data processed to calculate my average rating_” or “_I would like you to correct my rider rating per my rights under Article 16 of the GDPR_”
*** +Rationale+: Where a request mentions data protection law / personal data processing (even if it is confusing), Privacy should review it to double-check, as it falls directly under our remit of expertise.
*** +Privacy Response+: Escalate to Privacy. We will review and prepare the response.

[~accountid:712020:435d7fc1-7078-4aa9-b2a5-32758f7e11e4], we have completed an assessment of the privacy implications associated with engaging a data processor located in *Hong Kong (China)* in collaboration with external counsel. After evaluating the risks outlined below, we have reached the conclusion that it would not be advisable for Bolt to proceed with engaging the supplier or processor in Hong Kong (China). The key factors contributing to this recommendation include:

* Cross-Border Transfer Risks (Lack of Adequacy Decision)

Hong Kong (China) does not benefit from an adequacy decision by the European Union, meaning that the jurisdiction is not recognised as providing an equivalent level of data protection as required by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This lack of recognition complicates the cross-border transfer of personal data from the EU to Hong Kong, as additional safeguards would need to be implemented to ensure compliance. However, these measures, such as standard contractual clauses, are not foolproof and may not fully mitigate the risks involved in transferring data to a jurisdiction with lower data protection standards.

* Lack of Regulation for Data Processors in Hong Kong

Unlike the GDPR, which imposes specific obligations on data processors, Hong Kong’s Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO) lacks comprehensive regulatory requirements for data processors. This regulatory gap increases the risk that data processors in Hong Kong may not adhere to the same stringent data protection standards required under EU law. As a result, Bolt could face challenges in ensuring that its data processors in Hong Kong are fully compliant with its data protection obligations, potentially exposing the company to legal and reputational risks.

* No Data Breach Notification Requirement in Hong Kong

Hong Kong does not currently have a mandatory data breach notification requirement under the PDPO. This absence of a legal obligation to report data breaches poses a significant risk, as it may delay Bolt's awareness of any potential data breaches suffered by the supplier in Hong Kong, which could lead to severe consequences, including financial penalties and reputational damage reputation.

* Government Access and Surveillance Risks

One of the most concerning aspects of engaging a data processor in Hong Kong is the potential for government access and surveillance without adequate transparency or legal recourse. Cybersecurity Law and National Intelligence Law grant broad powers to the government for surveillance and data access. Despite any mitigation measures that we may put in place, it is not possible to eliminate the risk of governmental surveillance entirely.

Regarding *Germany*: 

The legal assessment on the use of dashcams in Germany remains unchanged from the previous advice. The German Data Protection Authorities are very restrictive about dashcam usage, often more so than the German Federal Court (BGH). While the BGH allows dashcam use within very narrow limits for evidence in accidents, requiring strict privacy measures like short recording times and automatic deletion, the Data Protection Authorities generally consider dashcam use unlawful due to privacy concerns.

BGH requirements: Dashcams may only be legally used if stringent technical measures are implemented, such as: (i) very short storage periods of the records, (ii) short-term, occasion-based recordings which are only activated by a motion sensor in the event of a collision or severe slow-down of the vehicle (60-120 seconds), (iii) pixelation of persons and (iv) automatic deletion outside the control of the dashcam user.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties (in particular, passengers). If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. [~accountid:712020:f1cea5d5-ecbb-422c-b79c-3378c160b57c] Thanks for bringing it to my attention yesterday that Drivers in Malaysia need to obtain an E-hailing Vehicle Permit (EVP) from APAD and that Bolt Malaysia will facilitate this. You mentioned that in doing so, Bolt will need to share data relating to the vehicle owner (car grant, car owner name, etc) and that there will be cases where a Driver doesn't actually own the vehicle — {{meaning that Bolt will need to share personal data of a 3rd party (the actual vehicle owner) with APAD}}.*_The Legal Issue_*

* We may be able to justify doing this if it is required by APAD ('Compliance with Legal Obligation') — if you can, please share a copy of the relevant Decree that sets out this obligation so that I can confirm this.
* We can also include wording in the Driver registration flow that requires Drivers to legally 'promise' that they have obtained the consent of the vehicle owner to share the car grant and car owner details with Bolt. This isn't perfect but I'd recommend we do it anyway as something to fall back on.
* {{We are still under a separate duty to notify those 3rd party vehicle owners that we are processing their personal data and will be sharing it with APAD}} — see [+Section 7+|https://www.pdp.gov.my/jpdpv2/assets/2019/09/Personal-Data-Protection-Act-2010.pdf] of the Malaysian Data Protection Law:

* This is typically done through a privacy notice.
* Bolt does not currently have a privacy notice for 3rd parties, like vehicle owners/emergency contacts/etc (except in Kenya). While we can draft one for Malaysia in time for the launch, your Team would still need to find a way to operationally 'communicate' the privacy notice to the 3rd party vehicle owners.

*_Recommendations_*

# I recommended that Drivers give those 3rd party vehicle owners a basic 'Form' to sign which confirms their consent to process and share their data with APAD, and includes a link to our privacy notice. {{You weren't too keen on this idea right now as it could potentially introduce friction to the driver onboarding flow, although I'm not sure how many Drivers we would estimate actually fall into this category (they don't own the car they are driving and registering with APAD)}}.
# We could also request Drivers to give us the 3rd party vehicle owners' email address, and we could then let them know (in writing - via email/SMS) that we have received their car grant and personal details from the Driver, and that we will be required to share it with APAD. We would also make reference to our Privacy Notice in this communication.

{noformat}Do you know how Grab is dealing with this compliance issue?{noformat}

*_The Risks_*

* If you decide to proceed without notifying those 3rd party vehicle owners that we collected their data from the Driver, and that we will process it and share it with APAD, we would be in breach of [+Section 7+ |https://www.pdp.gov.my/jpdpv2/assets/2019/09/Personal-Data-Protection-Act-2010.pdf]of the Malaysian Data Protection Law.
* Failure to comply with the provisions of the PDPA {{may amount to a criminal offense}}. Breaching the 'Notice and Choice' principle in Section 7 attracts a fine of up to MYR 300,000 (approx. $63,550) and/or two years imprisonment. If a corporate body is found to have committed an offense, {{the officers of such corporate bodies are deemed to have committed the offense personally}}.
* The Data Protection Authority in Malaysia (PDP) is active and has carried out recent enforcement action. In our case, this would likely only arise if a 3rd party vehicle owner complained to the PDP.

----

*BACKGROUND DETAILS ON SUPPLY BONUSES AND RECLASS RISK*

 As part of the reclassification mitigation plan in 2023 the following analysis was done in relation to *_Supply bonus_**:*

+_Situation prior to presumption of employment law for platform workers_+

_In order to encourage drivers to work more with us, we create time-limited campaigns that require them to fulfill some criteria in order to receive bonuses. Possible campaigns:_

# _Do x amount of rides by y hours, receive w€_
# _During the next x amount of time, we are paying y% more on every ride_
# _Be online for x amount of hours until tomorrow, receive y€_
# _Accept x% of the rides in the next y amount of hours, receive w€_

_Some drivers might be eligible for the bonuses while others aren’t (based on certain performance metrics / criteria - e.g. targeting part time drivers, drivers with low AR or inactive drivers for +30 days). This is communicated directly to drivers via the app, push notifications, text messages and emails._

+_Which reclassification criteria in the new presumption law we believe this might affect_+

* _Criteria 4 - By using OH and AR as criterias for them to earn more, we believe this might be seen as influencing their work schedule and/or the possibility of accepting or refusing tasks._
* _Criteria 1 - By defining bonuses at our discretion, we believe this might be seen as fixing the remuneration._
* _Criteria 2 - By defining specific areas where the bonuses apply, we believe this might be seen as exercising the power of direction._

+_What we plan to do for mitigation purposes_+

* _In a less risk-averse approach, we believe we can continue to offer bonuses based on KPIs but make them available to all drivers and avoid some of the criteria - e.g. keeping example 1. and 2. from “Current situation”._ 
* _As an intermediate solution, we could offer the bonus to the fleets and have them find a way to distribute it to drivers (e.g. bonus, reduced car rent, etc.)._
* _In a more risk-averse approach, we should stop bonuses all together._

+DLA feedback+: 

* Bonus should be only to the fleet, Bolt pays the bonus to the fleet and then the fleet pays the driver. Only the fleet should be incentivised. The whole bonus scheme should go to the fleet, not to the drivers.
* Or we can say that Bolt is running a campaign which should allow you, driver, to increase your earnings with the fleet → but this is not as mitigating.
* Suggestion from DLA: Someone who drives with Bolt can have a bonus, driver pls contact your fleet to know more.
* Major risk if anything is directly between Bolt and the driver.

→ We've always paid everything to the fleet. The bonus has the same setup internally (per driver ID) but we have changed the comms of these bonuses to make them seem more to the fleet and less to the driver (e.g. instead of "you earn x€" it would be "earning of x€").

I*N SUMMARY it was then decided that Bonus and incentive schemes should only be linked to cars and/or fleet owners (rather than drivers) and are being paid to fleet owners only (not drivers). KPIs such as Acceptance Rate should be avoided.*

This article is currently under PEX review, and we're working on further simplifying the process. I've also reviewed the templates from the related Legal SD:

{quote}{color:#4c9aff}*Scenario*{color}: If a driver has complained to us about their own account being compromised, then the ticket should remain open until we can be sure that the hacker no longer has access, they have regained access to their account, and we have resolved any other outstanding issues that the driver has.

“_Our specialist team has investigated this matter thoroughly and, to the extent that any unauthorised third party gained access to your account, appropriate steps have been taken to remove the third party and mitigate any adverse effects resulting from their access._ -_Please let us know if there are any additional issues that you wish to discuss, otherwise_--,- -_our team will consider this matter to be closed._-”{quote}

* We will add this template to the article. The wording is specific, which is important because we don't want agents mentioning anything beyond what's provided. However, I removed the last sentence. Asking users to contact us with additional questions goes against our quality standards, as we aim to resolve the issue fully before closing the case—so no further contact should be needed.

{quote}{color:#4c9aff}*Scenario*{color}: If a rider has complained to us about a driver’s account asking them for details that the rider finds suspicious, we should not be closing the ticket with the rider unless we are certain that the rider’s account has not itself become compromised as a result of the incident.

_“Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention. Our specialist team has investigated this matter thoroughly and has not seen anything to suggest that your account has been adversely affected as a result of this incident. Please let us know if there are any additional issues that you wish to discuss, otherwise, our team will consider this matter to be closed.”_{quote}

* This template can’t be technically added to the revamped process. If the rider reports phishing attempts, agents should follow the article [My account has unrecognised activity|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/70724]. Since we don’t have a Change log in the rider account, it’s hard to confirm whether their account was affected. Agents should therefore log the rider out of all their devices to ensure that only the phone number's owner can access the account. This will be done for all cases as a precautionary measure.

{quote}Dear XXX,

Thank you for your data subject rights request, which was received by us on *[DATE]* via a third party.

We are unable to authorise an attempted request submitted by the third party " Mine", obliging us to use its platform that is not one of our authorised suppliers having passed our internal due diligence processes.

To help us ensure the security of the personal data we hold about you and the genuineness of the instructions in respect of it, we need to verify any legal authority of that third party to act on your behalf.

In this instance, we request you to provide sufficient evidence of that third party’s legal authority to act on your behalf, for example:
·       a written consent signed by you as data subject;
·       a certified copy of a power of attorney;
·       or other proof of legal authority.

Please be aware that we are unable to respond to your request until we receive the additional information specified above upon your replying to this email.

Alternatively, please use one of the several channels available, such as requesting your data erasure directly via your application, or through your profile’s email request sent to our Customer Support Team.

We appreciate your cooperation in this matter and look forward to receiving the requested information from you.

Yours sincerely, Bolt{quote}



If consent/POA is not received, we send the following template to deny the request:

{quote}Dear [NAME],



We have been unable to verify the third party’s legal authority to make a request on your behalf. Therefore, we are unable to process your request to use an unauthorised third party application.



We ask you to raise a request by an alternative means - please use one of the several channels available, such as requesting your data erasure directly via your application, or through your profile’s email request sent to our Customer Support Team.



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them.



You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.



If you have any additional questions, please don't hesitate to reach out to our Support Team.



Yours sincerely, 

Bolt{quote}

Two approaches for the discussion, let’s call them “Pesimistic” & “Optimistic”

*“Pesimistic”* (proposed by Ivan and Andrei below)
- store event into DB as part of the payment updates transaction
- publish the event to SNS/SQS & mark it as published in the DB from the afterCommit hook
- have a cron running:
   - that will be publishing events that failed direct SNS publication
   - that will house-keep the table (delete successfully published events from the DB)
   - mark events that failed republishing as “failed” and keep them in the DB
*Pros:*
   - basically no chance that we would miss an event 
*Cons:*
   - it would get us closer to where we were with MqDbPublisher - all events going through the DB although for almost all of them it’s unnecessary


*“Optimistic”* (proposed by Michal below)

* tune-up SNS AWS client-lib build-in fail-and-retry mechanism
* publish the event to SNS/SQS & insert the event to the DB from the afterCommit hook in case of failure
* have a cron running:
** that will be publishing events that failed direct SNS publication
** mark events that failed republishing as “failed” and keep them in the DB

*Pros:*
   - doesn’t make all events to go through the DB, i.e. it doesn’t put unnecessary strain on the infra with all it’s MqDBPublisher like side-effects

*Cons:*

* In case SNS publishing fails and then we fail to insert the event into DB too for the retry then we would have to re-construct the event from the logs or otherwise


In either cases (Pessimistic as well as Optimistic) - we will need to find a way how to deal with events that can’t be published event from the re-try DB mechanism (e.g. because they are failing validation before they are published) - that has to be escalated to operator (alarm) in some way - the same mechanism we could use to cover the SNS & DB failed edge-case of the “Pesimistic” scenario.

And, yes - once this has been fixed we will have records to correct - I suppose we can dig out from presto booking item records in authorized state with payment records in captured state since end of March and re-publish those (basically put those events together from data we have e.g. in notifications table and build a job that publishes those events once).

Hi Gabrielé

 

Absolutely. I will try to clarify the Service, “BKY”, provided to Bolt by SvTF (Swedish Association of Taxi Operators) hopefully assure you that Personal Data is not disclosed or that any Information Regulations are breached.

 

“BKY” is a service under which an entity, such as Bolt, is allowed to access specific personal data directly linked to specific individuals. The personal data is stored in the Swedish Road Traffic Register, which is owned by, operated by and under the supervision of the Swedish Transport Authority, thus making the register for all intents and purposes a Register of the Swedish Government. The personal data information that can be accessed by an entity is restricted to information on drivers’ license or the validity of taxi licenses or permits. If a drivers’ license, taxi license or permit has been revoked the Entity is informed of such status, but not the reasons for such license or permit being revoked.

 

In order for an Entity, such as Bolt, to access the personal data information, an application has to be made to the Swedish Transport Authority which upon granting of such request enables the Entity to access such specific restricted personal data information of their drivers.

 

An entity can only access such information relating to drivers that perform services for the Entity and they may not access information of other individuals.

 

Furthermore, the Entity is not allowed to share or in any way disclose this information with other third parties.

 

Once Bolt was granted access to the Register, Bolt could access information relating to status of drivers’ licenses, taxi licenses and/or taxi permits for individuals or entities performing transport operations for and/or on behalf of Bolt.

 

This access to the Register is made possible by the Service “BKY” which acts as an intermediary between the Swedish Transport Authority and the Entity. Under a Framework Ageement between the Swedish Transport Authority and SvTF, SvTF is granted legal status as Information Intermediary.

 

This means that the Entity may access the requested information in the Road Traffic Register through the services of “BKY” who acts as an Intermediary only. Under the Agreement between the Swedish Transport Authority and SvTF, SvTF agrees to not store or in any way “process” such data but only serve as a ‘gateway’ for the information. Under no circumstances can SvTF be seen or regarded as ‘owner’ of such personal data and may not in any way process, store or disclose such personal data that legally ‘belongs’ to the Entity.

 

Under the Framework Ageement between the Swedish Transport Authority and SvTF whereby SvTF is granted legal status as Information Intermediary, SvTF is legally required to comply with all relevant legislation such as the European Unions (EU) General Data Protection Act. Should SvTF in any way breach said Act, or any other applicable legal code, SvTF may be held criminally liable for such breach or offence as well as legally required to fines issued by the Swedish Transport Authority and/or a criminal prosecutor as well as potential claims for damages.

 

Thus, with reference to the legal framework between SvTF and the Swedish Transport Authority I do believe that the specific issues on data information security can be resolved and that Bolt can satisfactorily be assured that such personal data is not disclosed, handled, stored or processed by SvTF.

 

Just let me know if you have any questions and I suggest we set up a Teamsmeeting so that we can work this one out.

 

Best regards

 

/Tommy Pilarp

Code to check what percentage of the providers we would drop, on average, for each eater cell:



{code:python}city_ids = load_model_info('live', 'v3.1/2024-08-30-12-11-20')['info']['cityIds']
global_cpo = pd.Series()
for city_id in city_ids:
    # exclude higher-res cities
    if city_id in [9, 13, 271, 297, 325]:
        continue
    print('city_id:', city_id)
    model = load_denormalized_data('live', 'v3.1/2024-08-30-12-11-20', city_id)
    provider_radius_lookup = model[1].set_index(0)[3]
    provider_radius_dict = provider_radius_lookup.to_dict()
    pdrc = model[0][['provider_id', 'car_dist_m', 'scooter_dist_m', 'bike_dist_m', 'h3_cell', 'providers_count']]
    pdrc['radius'] = pdrc['provider_id'].map(provider_radius_dict)
    
    pdrc_over = pdrc[(pdrc['car_dist_m'] > pdrc['radius'] * 1000) & (pdrc['scooter_dist_m'] > pdrc['radius'] * 1000) & (pdrc['bike_dist_m'] > pdrc['radius'] * 1000)]
    cells_over = pdrc_over['h3_cell'].value_counts().reset_index()
    cells_over.columns = ['h3_cell', 'over_radius_count']
    
    all_cells_over = pd.merge(pdrc[['h3_cell']].drop_duplicates(), cells_over, on='h3_cell', how='left')
    all_cells_over['over_radius_count'] = all_cells_over['over_radius_count'].fillna(0)

    cells_providers_count = pdrc[['h3_cell', 'providers_count']].drop_duplicates()
    cpo = pd.merge(cells_providers_count, all_cells_over, on='h3_cell', how='inner')
    cpo['removed_perc'] = cpo.apply(lambda row: row['over_radius_count'] / row['providers_count'] * 100, axis=1)
    
    print("p99:", cpo['removed_perc'].quantile(0.99))
    print("mean:", cpo['removed_perc'].mean())
    global_cpo = pd.concat([global_cpo, cpo['removed_perc']], ignore_index=True)
    
print(global_cpo.mean())
print(global_cpo.quantile(0.85))
{code}

“Dear Зураб,

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *5 August 2024*.

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties. Furthermore, we must point out that we are not required to disclose documents or otherwise provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

In your request, you specifically asked for the order history for the 23 April 2024. Therefore, we are providing the following information regarding the personal data we hold about you, to which you are entitled:

* *A file containing the order history of 23 April 2024.*

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our [https://bolt.eu/uk-ua/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/uk-ua/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides|smart-link], which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

*The Data Subject’s rights*

The Data Subject has the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning him or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws.

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email. 

 

Yours sincerely,

Bolt”

If statement (a) is more accurate, then *Bolt will still be technically sharing the information* with Louwmans, regardless of the fact that the drivers themselves will be inputting the information. In which case, this would need to be covered in a data processing / data sharing agreement.

If statement (b) is more accurate, then the driver would be sharing their information with Louwmans directly, and Bolt would not be involved in the arrangement (and so Bolt would not need to be party to any data processing / sharing agreement in this context).

*_(2) If the more accurate statement above is (a), how will the drivers be agreeing to sharing their information with Louwmans (and Louwman’s dealers)? Will this be through a checkbox, or signing up to an agreement, or something else?_*

As noted in the question, this is more relevant if statement (a) above is accurate, rather than statement (b).

Clause 3.0 of the [collaboration agreement|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GZSD3Hf8CIUxhXybjJlm1uGF4kintPBI5HT7QRMZm6c/edit] says “_By activating this offer by the participant in the Bolt platform, the lead will be passed on to the Toyota dealer responsible for this service area. By activating this, the participant agrees to the sharing of his contact details in accordance with the General Personal Data Regulation_”. Assuming that the “_participant_” here is the driver, *this is very unlikely to constitute valid consent* to the sharing of the driver’s contact details (as the driver is not party to the agreement). Instead, for more valid consent, we would need to ensure that drivers are +_actively_+ consenting to this data sharing (e.g., by ticking a box).

If the first option is more correct, then *this would not be categorised as ‘personal data’*, and so the requirements of the GDPR (including the need for a data processing / sharing agreement to cover this sharing) would not apply.

If this would involve any sending of promotional / marketing materials to drivers in an unsolicited way, then this may also trigger certain direct marketing law requirements. As such, please clarify the above so that I can check whether any analysis is needed on this point.

Depending on the answers to the above, this may impact whether we need to include any international data transfer mechanisms in any data processing / sharing agreement that we prepare.

[~accountid:5f0c30effe23000022252e68] apologies for the delay. Below the main points:

*What is Bolt sent*

* Bolt has an application that allows users to requests TVDE services, rent scooters, among other transportation services.
* Bolt would like to launch a new service for the delivery of goods/parcels.
* The user of the app will be able to request the delivery of packages to a recipient at a selected drop-off location by selecting the “Bolt Delivery'' category in the Bolt App. 
* TVDE operators registered in our platform may opt in to the “Bolt Delivery” category in the Bolt App, allowing them to provide this service in addition to the TVDE services. 
* For the delivery of the Package, the TVDE Operators enter into a Delivery Agreement directly with the user. The Delivery Agreement is deemed to be concluded from the moment the order for delivery of a Package is confirmed by the Driver via the Bolt App.
* By operating the Bolt App, Bolt acts only as a provider of the information society service (an intermediary) and is *not a party to the Delivery Agreement*. Bolt is not the provider of the delivery services. Bolt does not supervise, direct or control the manner in which the delivery of the Package is carried out by the Driver.

*What is included under postal services*

Postal services law (Lei n.º 17/2012, de 26 de Abril) clarifies in article 5 the following:

1 - A *postal item is the object, addressed in definitive form*, complying with the physical and technical specifications that allow it to be processed in a postal network, as *well as its delivery to the address indicated on the object itself or on its wrapping*, *namely*:
a) Mailing, which consists of written communication on a physical medium of any kind, including direct mail;
b) Books, catalogues, newspapers and other periodicals;
c) +*Postal parcel, which is a package containing goods or objects with or without commercial value.*+

This law does not foresee the innovative service that Bolt intends to launch. However, given the broad language under article 5(1)(c) of this law, we would like to confirm that “Bolt Delivery” does not enter in the scope of postal services and no authorization is necessary from ANACOM.

Thank you

Hey [~accountid:5f0c30effe23000022252e68] apologies for the delay. Local ops wants to launch “driver by the hour” in Portugal. We have seen a couple of months ago that TVDE law would not  block this category since TVDE Law states that rides can be priced by time. 

Due to fraud concerns, local ops team is considering the following:

* Clearly communicate to Drivers that they should end the ride before the end of the second hour.
* Increase pre-authorization amounts to ensure Riders have enough funds.
* Automatically send orders longer than two hours for price review, refunding the rider if the value exceeds €70.



In relation to this project could you please confirm you have discussed these plans with the tax, commerce and finance teams, namely concerning pre-authorization?

From legal point of view I have a few concerns:

* Where would it be clear to rider and driver at the time of selecting this category that there is a 2 hour limit? This limitation would need to be included in t&c and in the rider screen.
* What is the difference in credit card pre-autjorization between standard TVDE service and this new category? Generally, credit card pre-authorizations would require consent from user to avoid claims of abuse of law.
* How could we ensure compliance with the following requirements from TVDE law: 
** 4 - A plataforma eletrónica deve disponibilizar ao utilizador de um modo claro, percetível e objetivo, antes do início de cada viagem e durante a mesma:
a) A fórmula de cálculo do preço, indicando nomeadamente de forma discriminada o *preço total*, a taxa de intermediação aplicada e as tarifas aplicáveis, nomeadamente por distância, tempo e fator de tarifa dinâmica;
b) Uma *estimativa do preço da viagem a realizar*, calculada com base nos elementos fornecidos pelo utilizador e fatores de ponderação que compõem a fórmula de cálculo do preço a cobrar pelo operador do serviço.
…
6 - A plataforma eletrónica deve também disponibilizar para qualquer itinerário, em alternativa, uma proposta de preço fixo predeterminado, que, em caso de aceitação pelo utilizador, corresponde ao preço a cobrar no final do serviço independentemente da distância percorrida ou do tempo despendido.
* This category requires a review of t&c and app screens before deployment, which may take several weeks from legal side particularly if this is a new category not in use in other markets. Are you aware that is being done elsewhere to allow me to seek other colleagues from legal for support?

Thanks.

This one is not on the suppression list.

I can explain why it generally happens though:

*Background*

When an email fails to be delivered due to some reason (the email server is down, the address doesn’t exist and so on), it results in a bounce.

When sending emails we want to avoid them ending up in spam. For that not to happen, we need to maintain a good sender reputation. If we send out too many emails that bounce then it damages our sender reputation. AWS provides a suppression list for that case - if an email hard bounces then the address is added to our suppression list. This means we won’t send emails to that address anymore because those would also hard bounce and damage our sender reputation if we keep sending emails there.

*Our Cases*

I have mostly observed this happening for people who have left Bolt at some point and afterwards rejoined. When they leave, I suppose we close the email account, however we might still have some automation in place that keeps trying to send emails there. Of course the first such email would bounce and the email would end up in the suppression list.

The other theory I have is that for some new joiners perhaps someone already tries to send some emails before their email account has been opened. This would also result in a hard bounce and make the address end up in the suppression list.

Let me know if you have any questions about this.

FAQ

Q: Can the Payment OPS issue a refund? 
A: No, Payment OPS don't have an access to issue a refund in Beehive or in Admin. 

Q: I would like to issue a refund, but I don't have the necessary accesses. 
A: Your team lead should have permissions to issue refunds. Please escalate to them. If they are lacking any permissions then you can apply for the following in Admin. 
Rides: refund_payments, customer_support_beehive_ridehailing_order_refund
Delivery: Refund old orders (delivery_order_refund_extended) after 30 days
Rentals: rental_order_refund, rental_subscriptions_refund, rental_order_refund_city_fine
Carsharing: rental_car_order_refund
Bolt+: subscription_offer_customer_support

Q: Customer requests a refund to the original payment method. 
A: If you have already issued a refund to the Bolt Balance, but the customer is requesting a refund to OPM. You need to force the refund to Original payment method. We are not able to remove the balance. The customer will receive a double-refund. 

Q: Can I refund after Chargebacks?
A: No. If the customer has received a chargeback then we are not able to issue a refund. 

If this solved your issue then we will close the ticket in 48 hours. 
If you would still like the payment operations team to take a look at this issue then please leave a comment on the ticket and we will not close the case.

* If you can see a task with an error message _Invoice sum too small_: The invoice was not generated as the driver did not owe any commission to Bolt or he had more compensation than owed commission

That’s because their commission amount is negative, meaning we don’t have any commission to invoice.

This happens when driver’s compensations/campaigns are more than their commission. Since we deduct their compensations/campaigns from their commission, in that case they don’t have any commission to invoice.

The invoice is generated once their commission again exceeds their compensation/campaign/ ride discount sum. Then this invoice would cover the whole period without an invoice.

h3. Notes pre-meeting with Kish

*Beehive compensation guide*

This is the future of the compensation rules for all user personas, including Drivers. This project cannot be worked on without taking this into consideration. 

At the moment, compensation rules vary market by market depending on market set-up, conditions such as supply, market share, fraud patterns, etc. Due to all of these considerations it is highly unlikely that we will be able to achieve one set of global manual compensation guidelines. BUT, taking Beehive compensation guide into account, we don’t have to, since both the fraud metrics (not all! for now at least, check column L [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1BTMBP22Dj5bOEeobSMgrnwrApSvwTFk4y0icXWENYBI/edit?gid=0#gid=0]) and the refund ratio are configurable by market. All we have to achieve is the same actions taken by agents based on the signals from the Beehive compensation guide for Drivers. 

* For example, a driver in Croatia and a driver in Estonia request compensation for the same issue. Beehive compensation guide will potentially show different signals for these two cases to agents in Croatia and agents in Estonia, but they will still follow the same process (if fraud is yellow do this, if fraud is green do that, if gmv to refund ratio is low do this…). 

I would focus this project on making getting the Beehive compensation guide ready for Drivers and making sure the markets agree with the above mentioned approach - signals are configurable by market (in collaboration with Fraud & SuppX), but the same signal results lead to same action for agents globally. 

*Blockers/things to consider* 

# Beehive compensation guide is tied to issue tags. It doesn’t work properly if there is no issue tag added to the case. At the moment we don’t have a list of issue tags for Drivers that might result in a compensation being given, nor do we know if this list would be global or not. 

* Should we allow market-specific reasons (not) to compensate? IMO, it would be easiest if we had one set of issues we compensate for on all markets, and then allow market-specificities within the checks in the compensation guide (fraud & ratio). 

# Price reviews - it doesn’t seem like PRs will be shut down globally. They are done in Admin, and Beehive compensation guide doesn’t work in Admin. 

* There might be two possibilities:
** [Integrate Beehive comp. guide into PRs|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06QL08V5PB/p1724416611495479?thread_ts=1724399961.034309&cid=C06QL08V5PB]
** [Move PRs to Beehive |https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06QL08V5PB/p1725004884780119]
* What needs to be decided is what should be done regarding PRs within the scope of this project in case neither of the two possibilities happen (soon enough) & which options of the two listed we want to try to push

# (Not) deducting commission - at the moment commission is deducted or not deducted for certain issues on certain markets. On markets in which commission is deducted agents have to calculate is manually, which is not ideal. Additionally, dynamic commission is being tested which would make manual calculations more difficult or even impossible. This brings me to the conclusion that we need a global decision about whether we deduct commission and for exactly which issues, and this then needs to be automated in Beehive upon giving compensation to the driver. 

*Miscellaneous* 

As can be seen from [the document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KZUNCNkede4HdhEXODdXVyojltpJTFJ3_HF-4-gt0nA/edit#heading=h.3xx6tifidv58], _compensation_other_ is the top 1 compensation reason in 2024, with almost 1mil euros spent on it. I’ve spoken top contributor markets (FR, PL, PT), and they all compensate different things under this compensation reason. It’s clear that we need more granular compensation reasons for manual compensations. It would also make sense to tie them to issue tags.

Chances are your question has been already answered in the Knowledge Base.

FAQ

Q: Can the Payment OPS issue a refund? 
A: No, Payment OPS don't have an access to issue a refund in Beehive or in Admin. 

Q: I would like to issue a refund, but I don't have the necessary accesses. 
A: Your team lead should have permissions to issue refunds. Please escalate to them. If they are lacking any permissions then you can apply for the following in Admin. 
Rides: refund_payments, customer_support_beehive_ridehailing_order_refund
Delivery: Refund old orders (delivery_order_refund_extended) after 30 days
Rentals: rental_order_refund, rental_subscriptions_refund, rental_order_refund_city_fine
Carsharing: rental_car_order_refund
Bolt+: subscription_offer_customer_support

Q: Customer requests a refund to the original payment method. 
A: If you have already issued a refund to the Bolt Balance, but the customer is requesting a refund to OPM. You need to force the refund to Original payment method. We are not able to remove the balance. The customer will receive a double-refund. 

Q: Can I refund after Chargebacks?
A: No. If the customer has received a chargeback then we are not able to issue a refund. 

If this solved your issue then we will close the ticket in 48 hours. 
If you would still like the payment operations team to take a look at this issue then please leave a comment on the ticket and we will not close the case.

A: No, Payment OPS don't have an access to issue a refund in Beehive or in Admin. 

Q: I would like to issue a refund, but I don't have the necessary accesses. 
A: Your team lead should have permissions to issue refunds. Please escalate to them. If they are lacking any permissions then you can apply for the following in Admin. 
Rides: refund_payments, customer_support_beehive_ridehailing_order_refund
Delivery: Refund old orders (delivery_order_refund_extended) after 30 days
Rentals: rental_order_refund, rental_subscriptions_refund, rental_order_refund_city_fine
Carsharing: rental_car_order_refund
Bolt+: subscription_offer_customer_support

Q: Customer requests a refund to the original payment method. 
A: If you have already issued a refund to the Bolt Balance, but the customer is requesting a refund to OPM. You need to force the refund to Original payment method. We are not able to remove the balance. The customer will receive a double-refund. 

Q: Can I refund after Chargebacks?
A: No. If the customer has received a chargeback then we are not able to issue a refund. 

If this solved your issue then we will close the ticket in 48 hours. 
If you would still like the payment operations team to take a look at this issue then please leave a comment on the ticket and we will not close the case.

A: No, Payment OPS don't have an access to issue a refund in Beehive or in Admin. 

Q: I would like to issue a refund, but I don't have the necessary accesses. 
A: Your team lead should have permissions to issue refunds. Please escalate to them. If they are lacking any permissions then you can apply for the following in Admin. 
Rides: refund_payments, customer_support_beehive_ridehailing_order_refund
Delivery: Refund old orders (delivery_order_refund_extended) after 30 days
Rentals: rental_order_refund, rental_subscriptions_refund, rental_order_refund_city_fine
Carsharing: rental_car_order_refund
Bolt+: subscription_offer_customer_support

Q: Customer requests a refund to the original payment method. 
A: If you have already issued a refund to the Bolt Balance, but the customer is requesting a refund to OPM. You need to force the refund to Original payment method. We are not able to remove the balance. The customer will receive a double-refund. 

Q: Can I refund after Chargebacks?
A: No. If the customer has received a chargeback then we are not able to issue a refund. 

If this solved your issue then we will close the ticket in 48 hours. 
If you would still like the payment operations team to take a look at this issue then please leave a comment on the ticket and we will not close the case.

In our terms and conditions section 6.5 this is written in Hungarian: 

_”6.5 Mivel a Szolgáltatást a Társasággal szerződésben álló Szolgáltató teljesíti a saját nevében és javára, a Viteldíj is a Szolgáltatót illeti, ő a számla (nyugta) kiállítója és annak jogosultja is. Ennek értelmében a számla kiállítása a Szolgáltató felelőssége. A Társaság a fuvarközvetítésért az Utastól díjazásra nem jogosult. Ha az Utas számlát kér, akkor azt az adott fuvar végén közvetlenül a Sofőrtől kell kérnie.”_

+We don’t have this translated in english unfortunately, so this is my version of translation:+

_6.5 As the Service is provided by the Service Provider under contract with the Company in its own name and for its own account, the Fare is also due to the Service Provider, which is the issuer of the invoice (receipt) and the holder thereof. Accordingly, the Service Provider is responsible for issuing the invoice. The Company shall not be entitled to any remuneration from the Passenger for the carriage. If the Passenger requests an invoice, he/she must request it directly from the Driver at the end of the journey._

I’m still looking into the legal acts references and will get back to you as soon as I have them.

_Dear X,_

_Thank you for your understanding!_

_Best regards,_

_X - Bolt Support_
